thread.title: YouTube cracks down on disturbing children’s videos

author: Kari Paul
title: YouTube cracks down on disturbing children’s videos
text:
YouTube is limiting content the kinds of videos that children can see on its app following complaints from parents that kids were viewing alarming content on its YouTube Kids platform.
The company said Wednesday that it’s releasing new parental control options for the YouTube Kids app, which will allow guardians to select trusted channels for children to access starting this week. That means children can be restricted to channels that YouTube GOOG, +2.20% has verified as kid-friendly, including Sesame Workshop and PBS Kids. The company will approve more channels in the future.
Previously, YouTube’s autoplay feature was exposing children to violent videos disguised as kid-friendly content, including cartoons of Elsa from Disney’s DIS, -1.10% “Frozen” being buried alive or Spider-Man being tortured, according to the Verge . Often these would play automatically after legitimate videos on the site.
“While no system is perfect, we continue to fine-tune, rigorously test and improve our filters for this more open version of our app,” YouTube said in a blog post. “And, as always, we encourage parents to block and flag videos for review that they don’t think should be in the YouTube Kids app.”
Children’s advocates have taken aim at other tech companies as well lately, demanding that Facebook FB, +10.03% stop “targeting” kids with its Messenger app. Earlier this year activist shareholders asked Apple AAPL, +0.19% to make iPhones less addictive to children.
YouTube launched YouTube Kids in 2015 and since then has been criticized for inappropriate videos, including cartoons saying the world is flat , and has come under fire for privacy-related concerns. Previously YouTube relied on parents to flag inappropriate videos, but is now letting them change settings, giving them the ability to turn off YouTube’s autoplay function.
Creating a child-specific filter is an improvement over algorithmic filtering, which did not work, said Josh Golin, executive director of the Campaign for a Commercial-Free Childhood, told MarketWatch. The algorithmic filtering chose videos to automatically play based on similar subject matter.
“But more parental controls doesn’t absolve Google of its responsibility to keep inappropriate content off of YouTube Kids, regardless of whether families avail themselves of these new options,” he said.
He added that many children still watch the main YouTube platform rather than the kids’ app, which exposes them to “troubling” data collection practices. A Google spokeswoman previously said the company does not use data collected on children under 13 for personalization of ads.
“When a parent sets up a profile for their child, the only information collected is the name and birthday,” she said. “That input is then used to customize the experience.” She added, “Older kids will receive more text and more videos on the home screen.
Experts on children and digital media say parents should limit time on YouTube regardless of privacy and content restrictions. According to a 2016 recommendations put forth by the American Academy of Pediatrics, children under the age of 2 should be restricted from screen time completely while children ages 2 to 5 should get only up to one hour a day of quality programming. Children ages 6 and above should have screen time strictly monitored so they can get adequate sleep and outdoor time.
